# Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract">

###### Abstract

Agent skills can remarkably improve task success rates by using
human-written procedural documents, but their quality is difficult to
assess without environment-grounded verification. Existing skill
generation methods heavily rely on preference logs rather than direct
environment interaction, often yielding negligible or even degraded
gains. We identify that it is a fundamental timing bottleneck: robust
skills should be *posterior-based*, distilled from empirical environment
interaction rather than prior plans. In this study, we introduce the
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Posterior Distillation Index
(PDI)</span>, a trajectory-level metric that quantifies how well a
distilled skill is grounded in the task-environment evidence. To
operationalize PDI, we present
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SPARK</span>
(<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S</span>tructured
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">P</span>ipelines for
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>utonomous
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R</span>unnable
tas<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">K</span>s and
s<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">K</span>ill generation) for
preserving task execution evidence towards full trajectory-level
analysis. SPARK generates environment-verified trajectories used to
compute PDI, and it applies PDI as an online diagnostic and intervention
signal to ensure posterior skill formation. Across 86 runnable tasks,
SPARK-generated skills consistently surpass no-skill baselines and
outperform human-written skills on student models (inference cost up to
1,000$`\times`$ cheaper than teacher models). These findings show that
PDI-guided distillation produces efficient and transferable skills
grounded in the task-environment interaction. We release our code in
<a href="https://github.com/EtaYang10th/spark-skills"
class="ltx_ref ltx_href" target="_blank">SPARK</a>.

</div>

<div id="S1" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed on
wide-ranging interactive software
tasks \[<a href="#bib.bib3" class="ltx_ref"
title="ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models">25</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning">17</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib35" class="ltx_ref"
title="Led: llm enhanced open-vocabulary object detection without human curated data generation">30</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib36" class="ltx_ref"
title="Mˆ 3-bench: multi-modal, multi-hop, multi-threaded tool-using mllm agent benchmark">29</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref"
title="Learning from teaching regularization: generalizable correlations should be easy to imitate">7</a>\].
An emerging strategy is to equip agents with
*skills* \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>\],
defined as in-context procedural documents that encode task-specific
knowledge such as execution ordering, environment constraints, and
verifier contracts. Benchmarks \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillCraft: can LLM agents learn to use tools skillfully?">3</a>\]
demonstrate that prior-based, human-written skills can remarkably boost
task success rates, making such reusable procedural knowledge a
promising abstraction for building scalable agent systems.

</div>

<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Yet a pessimistic picture appears that the quality of these skills is
nearly impossible to assess without environment-grounded
verification \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>\].
Researchers propose lifelong skill
accumulation \[<a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="AutoSkill: experience-driven lifelong learning via skill self-evolution">24</a>\],
large-scale skill cataloging \[<a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillNet: create, evaluate, and connect AI skills">9</a>\], or
RL-based skill evolution \[<a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillRL: evolving agents via recursive skill-augmented reinforcement learning">22</a>\].
These studies lack trajectory verification and solely rely on preference
logs. As a result, they can not produce transferable skills between
teacher and student models at different capabilities. This raises a
fundamental question:

</div>

<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">What makes skill
distillation transferable across tasks and models efficiently and
reliably?</span>

</div>

<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">

We identify that a key bottleneck is the timing of skill formation
relative to the task-environment interaction. Existing skill
generation \[<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models">21</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillNet: create, evaluate, and connect AI skills">9</a>\] asks
the model to prescribe how a task should be solved before interacting
with the environment, yielding skills dominated by generic priors and
heuristics. Instead, we propose that effective procedural knowledge
should be *posterior-based* since its creation time: it must encode
environment-specific constraints, execution dependencies, and failure
modes discoverable only through environmental interactions. Once
distilled, this posterior experience becomes reusable and verifiable
guidance for future agent development.

</div>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x1.png" id="S1.F1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="660"
height="215" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1:
</span>PDI-based SPARK Illustration. <span id="S1.F1.6.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Left (Skill Generation)</span>:
Starting from a task description, a teacher agent (e.g., Claude Opus
4.6) interacts with a Dockerized environment (up to <span
class="math inline"><em>N</em><sub>max</sub></span> attempts) and
updates an exploration memo from execution feedback. Upon success, the
full trajectory trace is distilled into <span id="S1.F1.7.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span>. Upon failure, a
PDI-based proxy triggers targeted interventions. <span id="S1.F1.8.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) Right (Task Construction):</span> To
validate the quality of skill generation, this is a supporting pipeline
that converts prompt into oracle-verified benchmark instances via
blueprint generation and critique checks. Then, a student agent (e.g.,
GPT 5.4 mini) evaluates the generated skill on these independently
constructed tasks, testing whether PDI-grounded knowledge transfers
across tasks rather than overfitting to the teacher’s original
trajectory.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">

We introduce the <span id="S1.p5.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Posterior Distillation Index
(PDI)<span id="footnote1"
class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup>1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup>1</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote1.1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">1</span></span><span id="footnote1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">‘Posterior’ denotes knowledge distilled
from environment interaction. No probabilistic or Bayesian update is
assumed.</span></span></span></span></span> as a principled metric that
quantifies whether skills are grounded in environment-verified evidence
rather than purely prior-based plans. By design, PDI aggregates three
interpretable trajectory-level signals, including execution grounding,
plan copying, and memo ossification, using an equal-weight linear
combination. We deliberately avoid nonlinear fitting to ensure benchmark
independence. To operationalize PDI, we present <span id="S1.p5.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SPARK</span> (<span id="S1.p5.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S</span>tructured <span id="S1.p5.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">P</span>ipelines for <span id="S1.p5.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>utonomous <span id="S1.p5.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R</span>unnable tas<span id="S1.p5.1.7"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">K</span>s and s<span id="S1.p5.1.8"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">K</span>ill generation).
In <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>, SPARK serves dual
roles: it generates the environment-grounded trajectories from which PDI
is computed; and it uses PDI as an online intervention signal to improve
skill generation before its completion. Our main contributions are as
follows.

</div>

<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p6.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> <span id="S1.p6.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectory-verified Metric</span>: PDI
introduces a trajectory-level measure whether generated skills are
grounded in task-environment evidence rather than unverified prior
plans. PDI also provides a mechanistic assessment of which trajectories
yield truly transferable skills
(<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.5</span></a>).

</div>

<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p7.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> <span id="S1.p7.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill Generation</span>: SPARK makes
skill generation transparent and analyzable by preserving execution
logs, verifier signals, and memo histories towards full trajectory-level
analysis (<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.1.2 Exploration Memo ‣ 3.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.1.2</span></a>).

</div>

<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p8.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> <span id="S1.p8.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Online Intervention</span>: A memo-based
proxy of PDI enables an online monitoring and intervention during skill
exploration. Our primary <span id="S1.p8.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">with/without PDI</span> ablation
quantifies the performance gain enabled by this online intervention
(<a href="#S4.SS3" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.3 PDI Makes Autonomous Skill Generation Work ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.3</span></a>).

</div>

<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p9.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(4)</span> <span id="S1.p9.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectory Benchmark</span>: We provide a
trajectory-level benchmark with full execution traces, verifier signals,
memo histories, and distilled skills. This collected
environment-verified evidence allows for evaluating skill transfer
ability across environment interactions.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Agent skill acquisition and evaluation.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Agent skill acquisition has increasingly shifted from collecting
experiences to distilling and deploying skills across tasks.
Voyager \[<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models">21</a>\]
accumulates executable skills in an embodied environment.
ExpeL \[<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners">27</a>\] stores
natural-language lessons from prior failures. Growing attempts distill
the experience into transferable skill libraries, including
AutoRefine \[<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref"
title="AutoRefine: from trajectories to reusable expertise for continual LLM agent refinement">15</a>\],
Trace2Skill \[<a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Trace2Skill: distill trajectory-local lessons into transferable agent skills">12</a>\],
AutoSkill \[<a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="AutoSkill: experience-driven lifelong learning via skill self-evolution">24</a>\],
and CUA-Skill \[<a href="#bib.bib22" class="ltx_ref"
title="CUA-Skill: develop skills for computer using agent">4</a>\].
SkillRouter \[<a href="#bib.bib28" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillRouter: skill routing for LLM agents at scale">28</a>\]
further addresses the deployment by selecting highly-relevant skills
from large registries. Beyond skill acquisition, skill evaluation is
crucial to assess the quality of skills in real-world applications.
SkillsBench \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>\]
evaluates when curated skills help at inference time.
SkillWild \[<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref"
title="How well do agentic skills work in the wild: benchmarking LLM skill usage in realistic settings">10</a>\]
studies more realistic retrieval-and-adaptation settings. Unlike these
efforts, SPARK emphasizes interaction-grounded skill documents,
cross-instance skill transfer, and trajectory-level analysis.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### LLM agents with external feedback.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

SPARK follows the interact–reflect–retry line of agentic system
development, including ReAct \[<a href="#bib.bib3" class="ltx_ref"
title="ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models">25</a>\],
Reflexion \[<a href="#bib.bib4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning">17</a>\],
and ETO \[<a href="#bib.bib5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Trial and error: exploration-based trajectory optimization for LLM agents">19</a>\].
These studies mainly improve the decision making or trajectory revision
within a single task-solving episode (one attempt at completing a given
task). By contrast, we emphasize how agent execution traces can be
distilled \[<a href="#bib.bib1" class="ltx_ref"
title="Distilling the knowledge in a neural network">6</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib39" class="ltx_ref"
title="Born again neural networks">5</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref"
title="Learning from teaching regularization: generalizable correlations should be easy to imitate">7</a>\]
from the environment interaction that can transfer across tasks, turning
trial-and-error records into a reusable knowledge base.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Agent tooling and skill utility.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

LLM agent tooling and its transfer capability have evolved from learning
tool policies to structuring skills. For instance,
Toolformer \[<a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Toolformer: language models can teach themselves to use tools">16</a>\]
and ToolLLM \[<a href="#bib.bib7" class="ltx_ref"
title="ToolLLM: facilitating large language models to master 16000+ real-world APIs">14</a>\]
focus on learning to invoke tools. Meanwhile,
CREATOR \[<a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref"
title="CREATOR: tool creation for disentangling abstract and concrete reasoning of large language models">13</a>\]
and LATM \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref"
title="Large language models as tool makers">2</a>\] show that stronger
models can synthesize reusable artifacts for weaker ones. Skill-oriented
frameworks go further by packaging capabilities into modular,
self-contained units with clear invocation protocols.
SkillCraft \[<a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillCraft: can LLM agents learn to use tools skillfully?">3</a>\]
studies tool-usage skills,
SkillNet \[<a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillNet: create, evaluate, and connect AI skills">9</a>\]
organizes skills as reusable units, and
SkillX \[<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillX: automatically constructing skill knowledge bases for agents">20</a>\]
automatically constructs multi-level skill knowledge bases. In our
study, SPARK highlights that the transferred artifact is a
natural-language <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span> document rather
than the executable code.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We study whether distilled skills are grounded in environment-verified
evidence or merely reflect prior plans. To start, a teacher model
generates skills from environment-interacted trajectories for use by a
student model (here “teacher” denotes the behavior agent that produces
exploration trajectories and “student” is the agent that consumes the
learnable ones; no capacity asymmetry is implied). Our goal is to
measure when these trajectories yield transferable procedural knowledge.
We aim to define a trajectory-level score (i.e., Posterior Distillation
Index (PDI)) that measures the degree to which the generated skill
reflects posterior evidence rather than prior intent.
In <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>, SPARK produces major
trajectories for PDI computation and uses PDI as an online signal to
improve skill generation during the time of skill exploration. We
describe skill generation
(<a href="#S3.SS1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.1</span></a>) and task
construction pipeline
(<a href="#S3.SS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.2</span></a>) that enables this
trajectory-level skill exploration.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Skill Generation Pipeline

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

In <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a> left,
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span> the teacher agent
interacts with a Dockerized environment up to $`N_{\max}`$ attempts. At
each attempt, <span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.3.pic2" class="ltx_picture" /></span> teacher agent issues
shell commands and observes terminal output. Then
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.4.pic3" class="ltx_picture" /></span> teacher agent
produces a *Terminal Interaction Log* and *Evaluation Record*.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.5.pic4" class="ltx_picture" /></span> When an attempt
succeeds from the evaluator, <span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.6.pic5" class="ltx_picture" /></span> the full trajectory
is distilled into a reusable document <span id="S3.SS1.p1.7.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span>
(<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.1.1 Evidence-Driven Skill Generation ‣ 3.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.1.1</span></a>); when it fails,
the structured *exploration memo*
(<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.1.2 Exploration Memo ‣ 3.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.1.2</span></a>) is updated to
capture the resulting evidence and revise the next strategy. This
closed-loop design makes the generated skill explicitly traceable to the
environment interaction. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.p1.7.pic6" class="ltx_picture" /></span> Next, the Posterior
Distillation Index (PDI,
<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.5</span></a>) is computed to
quantify whether the accumulated trajectory is grounded in
environment-verified evidence. Notably, PDI is not only a retrospective
diagnostic signal since a proxy-based PDI can trigger intervention
during skill exploration. This makes PDI useful both for trajectory
analysis and improving skill generation online. Below we detail major
blocks of evidence-driven skill generation and exploration memo. A full
procedure is provided in <a href="#A8.SS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="H.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ Appendix H Pipeline Pseudocode ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1</span></span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Evidence-Driven Skill Generation

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

When a task is accomplished, SPARK assembles six structured evidence
blocks to provide the skill-generation model with a comprehensive view
of the solution path and obstacle encountered. This multi-source
evidence design allows the generated skill toward reusable procedural
structure rather than task-instance surface form, while establishing an
explicit interface for evaluating predictive validity of individual
evidence sources with respect to downstream skill utility.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

In <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a> left:
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Task
Pattern</span> is a condensed task instruction capturing the problem
class. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2)
Execution Chain</span> offers key commands from the successful attempt,
after semantic classification, importance scoring, and low-signal
filtering. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Verification</span> records tests
passed and the final reward. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4) Lessons</span> store repeated failure
patterns and confirmed cautions distilled from the full attempt history.
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5)
Environment</span> offers runtime context from the Dockerfile (base
image, packages, SDKs). <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6) Raw Support Tail</span> shows the tail
of the agent’s stdout from the successful run.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Exploration Memo

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

A single agent attempt can produce excessive amounts of tokens of raw
stdout (standard output) and shell commands. Carrying this history
forward verbatim would quickly exhaust the context window and dilute the
model’s attention. We therefore introduce the *exploration memo* as a
structured summary state that the teacher agent maintains across
attempts. This design keeps the exploration process interpretable while
preventing low-value repetition from overwhelming the context window.
After each failed attempt, the teacher agent *completely rewrites* the
memo using recent agent’s commands and a structured test summary, rather
than appending to the old version. The memo follows a fixed five-section
structure as shown in the left part of
<a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>:

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

Notably, we preserve the full historical memo so that cross-attempt
patterns remain available for subsequent analysis. SPARK’s
exploration-quality techniques are summarized in
<a href="#A8.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="H.2.1 Integrated Techniques for Exploration Quality ‣ H.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ Appendix H Pipeline Pseudocode ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.1</span></span></a>.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Task Construction Pipeline

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

In <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a> right,
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span> task-construction
pipeline converts a prompt-level task idea into a structured task
blueprint via three sequential stages.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.2.pic2" class="ltx_picture" /></span> A blueprint stage
that exposes explicit intermediate structure;
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.3.pic3" class="ltx_picture" /></span> a repair stage that
iteratively fixes violated constraints in the blueprint;
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.4.pic4" class="ltx_picture" /></span> a critique stage
that checks semantic consistency and executable constraints; and
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.5.pic5" class="ltx_picture" /></span> a validation stage
that accepts only tasks passing deterministic oracle verification.
Overall, task generation is a build-and-verify process that ensures each
generated task is self-contained rather than a single-LLM-generated
step. Further, <span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS2.p1.6.pic6" class="ltx_picture" /></span> the pipeline
supports cross-instance transfer evaluation by constructing unseen task
variants from high-level specifications, on which a student agent is
then deployed to test whether skills distilled from one trajectory
generalize to related but independently constructed tasks.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We adopt the task suite from the SkillsBench
benchmark \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>\],
which provides 86 tasks spanning 11 domains (e.g., Software Engineering,
Finance, and Cybersecurity), each paired with a natural-language
instruction, a Docker execution environment, and a deterministic pytest
oracle. To broaden our evaluation, SPARK
(<a href="#S3.SS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.2</span></a>) can synthesize
runnable task variants from natural-language prompts; we use this
capability to extend the evaluation pool (n = 300) and validate the
generality power (<a href="#S4.SS4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.4 Ablation Study on Task Variants ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.4</span></a>). For cross-domain
generalization, we evaluate SPARK on
ALFWorld \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref"
title="ALFWorld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">18</a>\],
a text-based household environment differing from terminal-based
programming tasks. A capable teacher model interacts with the
environment over up to $`N_{\max}{=}7`$ attempts; the objective is to
distill the procedural knowledge embedded in these interactions into a
reusable skill document that improves a weaker student model (statistics
are reported in <a href="#A7" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix G Exploration Statistics ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></span></a>). The human-written
skills used as a comparison baseline are those provided by
SkillsBench \[<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks">8</a>\];
we use them as-is without modification.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Evaluation metrics.

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Each task is associated with a deterministic pytest oracle that returns
a reward $`r\in[0,1]`$, where $`r{=}1`$ indicates full task completion.
We report two quantities throughout the study:
<span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">task
reward</span> $`r_{m,t}`$, namely the reward obtained by student model
$`m`$ on task $`t`$ under a given condition (baseline, with SPARK skill
or with human-written skill); and <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.8.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">skill gain</span>
$`\Delta r_{m,t}=r_{m,t}^{\text{+skill}}-r_{m,t}^{\text{base}}`$, namely
the change in the reward attributable to the skill, where positive
values indicate improvement and negative values indicate degradation. We
aggregate across tasks via the mean reward
$`\bar{r}_{m}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t}r_{m,t}`$ and the mean
skill gain
$`\overline{\Delta r}_{m}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t}\Delta r_{m,t}`$.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Main Results

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F3.3"
class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top"
style="width:247.2pt;">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x2.png" id="S4.F3.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="471" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Mean
reward <span class="math inline"><em>r̄</em></span> across seven student
models under three conditions: no skill (baseline), SPARK-generated
skills, and human-written skills. Horizontal dotted lines mark the
interaction-free performance of two strong teacher models.</figcaption>
</figure>
</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F3.6"
class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top"
style="width:175.6pt;">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x3.png" id="S4.F3.4.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" width="830"
height="720" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3:
</span>Cross-model agreement rate <span
class="math inline"><em>A</em>(<em>m</em><sub><em>i</em></sub>, <em>m</em><sub><em>j</em></sub>)</span>
among seven student models. Off-diagonal values are generally
moderate.</figcaption>
</figure>
</div>
</div>
</figure>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a> reports the mean reward
$`\bar{r}`$ of seven student models under three conditions: no skill
(baseline), SPARK-generated skills, and human-written skills. Two
horizontal lines mark the unaided performance of GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus
4.6 as the teacher models used during exploration.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Two striking findings stand out. <span id="S4.SS1.p2.5.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First</span>, SPARK-generated skills
consistently outperform human-written skills on the majority of student
models: for instance, GPT-5.4-mini guided by SPARK skills reaches
$`\bar{r}{=}0.52`$, surpassing the human-written condition ($`0.47`$).
<span id="S4.SS1.p2.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Second</span>,
several small student models equipped with SPARK skills exceed the
unaided performance of the teacher models themselves. For instance,
GPT-5.4-nano with SPARK skills ($`0.41`$) outperforms Claude Opus 4.6
without skills ($`0.37`$). Overall, SPARK-distilled skills capture
environment-specific insights that strong models alone miss,
substantially narrowing the gap between weaker and stronger models.
SPARK also carries a favorable cost profile: although strong-teacher
exploration is expensive (<a href="#A7" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix G Exploration Statistics ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></span></a>), the upfront cost
amortizes across repeated cheap student runs—student inference costs as
little as \$0.02 per task, over $`1{,}000\times`$ cheaper than teacher
exploration—in some cases enabling weaker students to even surpass the
teacher’s own interaction-free performance.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Trajectory-Level Analysis

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Although SPARK-generated skills improve student performance
(<a href="#S4.SS1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.1</span></a>), they do not reveal
*why* some trajectories yield useful skills while others do not. Our
central answer is the Posterior Distillation Index (PDI), which measures
whether a distilled skill is grounded in posterior execution evidence
rather than stale prior plans. Before formalizing PDI in
<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.5</span></a>, we first
establish key motivating observations below
(<a href="#A2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix B Trajectory Feature Correlation Analysis ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></span></a> details further
trajectory correlation analysis).

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1 </span><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-4.0pt;"><img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/figure/Q.png" id="S4.SS2.SSS1.1.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" width="25" height="28"
alt="[Uncaptioned image]" /></span> Do a Few High-Quality Skills Drive All Gains?

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

For each pair $`(m_{i},m_{j})`$, we restrict to tasks where both fail
the baseline ($`r^{\mathrm{base}}_{m,t}{=}0`$) and at least one shows a
non-zero skill-induced change, and define the agreement rate as
$`A(m_{i},m_{j})=\frac{\bigl|\{t\mid\mathrm{sign}(\Delta r_{m_{i},t})=\mathrm{sign}(\Delta r_{m_{j},t})\}\bigr|}{\bigl|\{t\mid\Delta r_{m_{i},t}\neq 0\lor\Delta r_{m_{j},t}\neq 0\}\bigr|}`$.
<a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a> shows that off-diagonal
rates are only moderate ($`<`$<!-- -->60%). This calls for
trajectory-level predictors of skill quality across models at different
capacities.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.2 </span><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-4.0pt;"><img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/figure/Q.png" id="S4.SS2.SSS2.1.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" width="25" height="28"
alt="[Uncaptioned image]" /></span> Does More Evidence or More Attempts Improve Skills?

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

We next ask whether *quantitative* factors alone, such as the volume of
exploration evidence or the number of attempts, are sufficient to
determine skill quality.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Compression ratio.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Let $`L_{\mathrm{traj}}`$ denote the total character length of the
agent’s execution outputs (stdout) across all attempts, and
$`L_{\mathrm{skill}}`$ the character length of the distilled
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.8.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span>. We define the
compression ratio as $`\rho_{c}=L_{\mathrm{traj}}/L_{\mathrm{skill}}`$.
<a href="#S4.F4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 4 ‣ Exploration-mode classification. ‣ 4.2.3 Does Convergent or Divergent Exploration Produce Better Skills? ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a> (left) plots
$`\rho_{c}`$ (log scale) against per-pair $`\Delta`$reward for all
baseline-unsolved student$`\times`$task pairs. Across most student
models, the Spearman correlation between $`\rho_{c}`$ and
$`\Delta`$reward is negative, indicating that excessive compression
discards actionable details and degrades skill effectiveness.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Exploration attempt budget.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

For each task, let $`K`$ denote the number of execution attempts the
teacher performed before skill generation. For each student model $`m`$,
we group all baseline-unsolved tasks by $`K`$ and compute the mean skill
gain per bin as
$`\overline{\Delta r}_{m}(K)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{m,K}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{m,K}}\Delta r_{m,t}`$,
where $`\mathcal{T}_{m,K}`$ is the set of tasks for which student model
$`m`$ fails the baseline and the teacher uses exactly $`K`$ attempts.
<a href="#S4.F4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 4 ‣ Exploration-mode classification. ‣ 4.2.3 Does Convergent or Divergent Exploration Produce Better Skills? ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a> (middle) shows that
gains are positive and relatively stable for $`K\leq 3`$, but become
volatile and model-dependent beyond that point. More exploration
therefore does not by itself explain why a distilled skill becomes
useful.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.3 </span><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-4.0pt;"><img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/figure/Q.png" id="S4.SS2.SSS3.1.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" width="25" height="28"
alt="[Uncaptioned image]" /></span> Does Convergent or Divergent Exploration Produce Better Skills?

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

We next ask whether the instability above depends on *how* the teacher
explores, namely whether it stays within one line of attack or pivots to
different ones.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Exploration-mode classification.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Let $`\mu_{i}`$ denote the memo text after the $`i`$-th reflection. We
measure the Jaccard similarity between successive memos as
$`J_{i}=\frac{|\,\mathrm{tok}(\mu_{i-1})\cap\mathrm{tok}(\mu_{i})\,|}{|\,\mathrm{tok}(\mu_{i-1})\cup\mathrm{tok}(\mu_{i})\,|}`$,
where $`\mathrm{tok}(\cdot)`$ denotes word-level tokenization. We then
fit a linear trend $`J_{i}\approx\alpha+\gamma\cdot i`$ and use the
slope $`\gamma`$ to classify each task:
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1.8.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Convergent</span> ($`\gamma>0`$), where
successive memos become increasingly similar, and
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p1.8.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Divergent</span> ($`\gamma\leq 0`$),
where memos grow less similar over time.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#S4.F4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 4 ‣ Exploration-mode classification. ‣ 4.2.3 Does Convergent or Divergent Exploration Produce Better Skills? ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a> (right) reports the
mean skill gain $`\overline{\Delta r}`$ for each student model, grouped
by exploration mode. Across nearly all student models, skills distilled
from divergent trajectories yield substantially larger gains than those
from convergent ones; for several models, convergent-trajectory skills
even produce negative $`\Delta r`$ relative to the no-skill baseline.

</div>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<div id="S4.F4.1"
class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top"
style="width:110.4pt;">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x4.png" id="S4.F4.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="640" alt="Refer to caption" />
</div>
</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<div id="S4.F4.2"
class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top"
style="width:120.8pt;">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x5.png" id="S4.F4.2.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="585" alt="Refer to caption" />
</div>
</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<div id="S4.F4.3"
class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top"
style="width:110.4pt;">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x6.png" id="S4.F4.3.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="642" alt="Refer to caption" />
</div>
</div>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Three
complementary views of skill quality determinants. <span id="S4.F4.15.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> Compression ratio <span
class="math inline"><em>ρ</em><sub><em>c</em></sub></span> vs. per-pair
<span class="math inline"><em>Δ</em><em>r</em></span>; excessive
compression degrades skill effectiveness. <span id="S4.F4.16.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Middle:</span> Mean <span
class="math inline"><em>Δ</em><em>r</em></span> as a function of the
number of exploration attempts; gains are stable for the first three
attempts and become volatile thereafter. <span id="S4.F4.17.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> Mean <span
class="math inline">$\overline{\Delta r}$</span> per student model for
skills distilled from convergent vs. divergent teacher
trajectories.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">

This contrast reveals that exploration quality depends not only on
search volume, but also on whether the trajectory accumulated genuinely
new posterior evidence rather than refining the same plan.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.4 </span><span id="S4.SS2.SSS4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-4.0pt;"><img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/figure/Q.png" id="S4.SS2.SSS4.1.1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" width="25" height="28"
alt="[Uncaptioned image]" /></span> What Separates Useful Iterative Skills from Useless Ones?

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

Prior analyses motivate us to hypothesize that useful skills emerge when
the final document distills posterior execution evidence rather than
echoing prior plans. We call this property the Posterior Distillation
Index (PDI) (<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.5</span></a>). To formalize it,
we compare *token-frequency distributions* between trajectory segments
and the final skill to capture both token presence and its emphasis.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Token-distribution setup.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

For any text segment $`x`$ and a fixed vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$
constructed from the trajectory, let $`c_{x}(w)`$ denote the count of
token $`w`$. We define the additively smoothed empirical distribution
$`P_{x}(w)=\frac{c_{x}(w)+\alpha}{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}c_{x}(v)+\alpha|\mathcal{V}|},\qquad\alpha>0`$.
To measure how probability mass shifts between trajectory segments and
the final skill, we need a discrepancy that is sensitive to token
*frequency*, not merely token *presence*. The Kullback–Leibler (KL)
divergence $`\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,Q)=\sum_{w}P(w)\log\frac{P(w)}{Q(w)}`$
is a natural candidate: it quantifies the coding inefficiency of using
$`Q`$ to represent $`P`$. However, KL is asymmetric and unbounded, which
complicates interpretation when neither distribution is a clear
reference. We thus adopt the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), a
symmetrized and bounded variant:

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\mathrm{JS}(P_{x},P_{y})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{KL}(P_{x}\,\|\,M)\;+\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{KL}(P_{y}\,\|\,M),\qquad M=\tfrac{P_{x}+P_{y}}{2}\,,
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span> |

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">

which lies in $`[0,1]`$ under base-2 logarithms. JSD inherits KL’s
sensitivity to how probability mass is allocated across tokens, while
remaining symmetric and well-defined even for sparse distributions. We
convert divergence to similarity via
$`\psi(P_{x},P_{y})=1-\mathrm{JS}(P_{x},P_{y})`$, so that higher values
indicate stronger distributional alignment. We examine three dynamic
properties of each trajectory below:

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="S4.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Plan
  Copying</span> ($`\phi_{\mathrm{plan}}`$). Let $`P_{P}`$ denote the
  token distribution of all accumulated *Next Strategy* sections from
  the exploration memo, and $`P_{s}`$ the token distribution of the
  final <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.5.3"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span>. We define plan
  copying as $`\phi_{\mathrm{plan}}=\psi(P_{P},P_{s})`$. High
  $`\phi_{\mathrm{plan}}`$ indicates that the skill’s token emphasis
  closely mirrors the memo’s planned actions rather than encoding
  independently verified knowledge.

  </div>
- <span id="S4.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Execution
  Grounding</span> ($`\phi_{\mathrm{exec}}`$). Let $`P_{E}`$ denote the
  distribution of agent commands from the successful execution trace. We
  define execution grounding as
  $`\phi_{\mathrm{exec}}=\psi(P_{E},P_{s})`$. High
  $`\phi_{\mathrm{exec}}`$ indicates that the skill concentrates on
  operations by operations validated by the environment.

  </div>
- <span id="S4.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memo
  Ossification</span> ($`\phi_{\mathrm{oss}}`$). We measure two
  cross-attempt stability signals: (i) the distributional similarity of
  *Verified Facts* between consecutive reflections,
  $`\psi(P_{v_{i-1}},P_{v_{i}})`$, and (ii) the distributional
  persistence of failed test sets, $`\psi(P_{f_{i-1}},P_{f_{i}})`$. We
  define memo ossification as the equal-weight average
  $`\phi_{\mathrm{oss}}=\frac{1}{2}\,\overline{\psi(P_{v_{i-1}},P_{v_{i}})}+\frac{1}{2}\,\overline{\psi(P_{f_{i-1}},P_{f_{i}})}`$,
  where $`\overline{(\cdot)}`$ denotes the mean across consecutive
  attempt pairs. High $`\phi_{\mathrm{oss}}`$ indicates that the
  trajectory is stuck, repeating the same task understanding and failure
  patterns without substantive update.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.5 </span>Posterior Distillation Index (PDI)

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">

We aggregate above three characteristics into a single composite score.
Let $`z(\cdot)`$ denote z-score normalization across all iterative
tasks. The *Posterior Distillation Index* (PDI) is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\mathrm{PDI}\;=\;z(\phi_{\mathrm{exec}})\;-\;z(\phi_{\mathrm{plan}})\;-\;z(\phi_{\mathrm{oss}})\,.
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span> |

Intuitively, a high PDI indicates that the skill is distributionally
aligned with environment-verified evidence (high
$`\phi_{\mathrm{exec}}`$), diverges from memo-level plans (low
$`\phi_{\mathrm{plan}}`$), and stems from a trajectory whose task
understanding genuinely evolves rather than repeating the same failure
pattern (low $`\phi_{\mathrm{oss}}`$). We intentionally use a simple
equal-weight linear form because PDI is designed to be an
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS5.p1.8.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">interpretable</span> and
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS5.p1.8.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">transferable</span> diagnostic index
rather than a benchmark-specific predictive model. Indeed,
sign-consistent weight combinations yield significant correlations
($`p{<}0.05`$) with skill gain, and cross-validated weight fitting
underperforms on held-out data (<a href="#A6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix F Sensitivity of PDI to Component Weights ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></span></a>), confirming that PDI’s
predictive power derives from its directional structure rather than any
particular coefficient. Throughout the experiments, we instantiate PDI
with $`\mathcal{D}{=}\mathrm{JS}`$ and a smoothing parameter
$`\alpha{=}0.002`$; sensitivity to $`\alpha`$ is analyzed below.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### PDI predicts student-level gains.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate the predictive power of PDI through three complementary
views (<a href="#S4.F5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 5 ‣ PDI predicts student-level gains. ‣ 4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a>), each targeting a
different facet of skill usefulness.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">

*Panel (a): Pass-gain rate.* For each trajectory group
$`g\in\{\text{interaction-free},\allowbreak\,\text{iter-low-PDI},\allowbreak\,\text{iter-high-PDI}\}`$
and student model $`m`$, we compute the pass-gain rate over
baseline-unsolved pairs as
$`\mathrm{PG}(g,m)=\frac{\bigl|\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{g}\mid r_{m,t}^{\text{base}}{=}0\wedge r_{m,t}^{\text{+skill}}{=}1\}\bigr|}{\bigl|\{t\in\mathcal{T}_{g}\mid r_{m,t}^{\text{base}}{=}0\}\bigr|}`$,
where $`\mathcal{T}_{g}`$ denotes the set of tasks in trajectory group
$`g`$. This quantity is the probability that a student passes with the
skill given that it failed without one. Skills from high-PDI iterative
trajectories consistently achieve the highest pass-gain rates across all
seven student models, outperforming both interaction-free skills and
low-PDI iterative skills, the latter of which often fall below 0.10.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">

*Panel (b): PDI vs. skill gain.* For each baseline-unsolved iterative
pair $`(m,t)`$, we plot PDI against the skill gain $`\Delta r_{m,t}`$.
The scatter reveals a significant positive Spearman correlation
($`\rho{=}{+}0.364`$, $`p{=}4.7{\times}10^{-7}`$): higher PDI is
associated with larger student gains across student models.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">

*Panel (c): Memo ossification vs. gap to human skills.* We define the
gap relative to human-written skills as
$`G_{m,t}=\Delta r_{m,t}^{\text{SPARK}}-\Delta r_{m,t}^{\text{human}}`$,
where $`\Delta r_{m,t}^{\text{SPARK}}`$ and
$`\Delta r_{m,t}^{\text{human}}`$ are the skill gains from
SPARK-generated and human-written skills, respectively. Plotting
$`\phi_{\mathrm{oss}}`$ against $`G_{m,t}`$ yields a negative
correlation ($`\rho{=}{-}0.277`$, $`p{=}1.6{\times}10^{-4}`$),
confirming that cognitive stagnation during exploration directly harms
downstream transfer.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para">

A Mann–Whitney U test between high- and low-PDI task groups yields
$`p{=}0.028`$, confirming that PDI retains discriminative power at the
task level.

</div>

<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x7.png" id="S4.F5.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="206" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5:
</span>Trajectory-level analysis of skill quality using divergence-based
PDI (<span class="math inline"><em>α</em> = 0.002</span>). (a) Pass-gain
rate by trajectory group across seven student models: high-PDI iterative
trajectories consistently outperform both interaction-free and low-PDI
iterative skills. (b) PDI vs. per-pair <span
class="math inline"><em>Δ</em><em>r</em></span> (<span
class="math inline"><em>ρ</em> = +0.364</span>, <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> &lt; 10<sup>−6</sup></span>). (c) Memo
ossification vs. gap relative to human-written skills (<span
class="math inline"><em>ρ</em> = −0.277</span>, <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> &lt; 10<sup>−3</sup></span>):
trajectories that repeat stale task understanding produce skills that
fall further behind human baselines.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 2:
</span>Ablation results on downstream pass rate and task-variant
transfer. Left: pass rate on the PDI-rerun task subset under skills
generated without and with PDI-guided online intervention. Right:
transfer to 300 additional runnable task variants generated by the
layered task-construction pipeline.</figcaption>
</figure>
</div>
</figure>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

To disentangle the contributions of plan copying and execution
grounding, we partition iterative tasks into four quadrants by the
median of $`\phi_{\mathrm{plan}}`$ and $`\phi_{\mathrm{exec}}`$.
<a href="#S4.T1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 1 ‣ Effective skills ground in evidence rather than plans. ‣ 4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a> reports the mean
$`\Delta r`$ and the mean gap versus human-written skills for each
quadrant. The best-performing quadrant, low plan copying combined with
high execution grounding, achieves a mean $`\Delta r`$ of
$`+`$<!-- -->0.377 and a positive gap of $`+`$<!-- -->0.312 over human
skills. In contrast, the worst quadrant, high plan copying with low
execution grounding, yields a near-zero mean $`\Delta r`$ of
$`+`$<!-- -->0.028 and a gap of $`-`$<!-- -->0.040 below human skills.
This confirms that useful skills are not summaries of what the agent
*planned* to do, but distillations of what the environment *verified* to
work.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Belief stagnation undermines exploration.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

A related failure mode is what we term the *facts–strategy gap*: the
difference between the cross-attempt stability of *Verified Facts* and
*Next Strategy*. A large gap indicates that the agent superficially
varies its strategy across retries while its task understanding remains
unchanged, a form of pseudo-exploration. Among iterative tasks, this gap
is negatively correlated with mean $`\Delta`$reward
($`\rho{=}{-}0.390`$, $`p{=}0.033`$), confirming that trajectories in
which “strategies change but task understanding does not” fail to
produce transferable skills.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Sensitivity to the smoothing parameter.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS5.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

PDI is robust to the choice of $`\alpha`$ within a broad low-smoothing
regime; the full sensitivity curves and significance analysis are
provided in <a href="#A5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix E Sensitivity of PDI to the Smoothing Parameter ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></span></a>.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>PDI Makes Autonomous Skill Generation Work

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

The above analyses treat PDI as a descriptor applied to completed
trajectories. A natural question is whether the same signal can improve
autonomous skill generation <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">during</span> the process itself. To
test this, we rerun skill generation, with PDI-guided online
intervention explicitly enabled, on the subset of tasks where original
trajectories showed persistently low proxy-PDI values. To avoid
introducing confounding effects, this subset excludes tasks where the
teacher agent succeeded in the first round and those where the PDI
monitors remain within healthy thresholds that will not trigger
interference.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

Concretely, after each reflect step $`k`$ SPARK computes a weighted
proxy-PDI $`\hat{d}_{k}=w_{k}\cdot\mathrm{PDI}_{k}`$, where
$`w_{k}=\min(1,\,k/W)`$ is a linear warm-up ramp ($`W{=}2`$) that
suppresses noisy early signals. When $`\hat{d}_{k}<\tau`$
($`\tau{=}{-}0.5`$), a *soft* intervention injects prompt-only guidance
encouraging broader hypothesis revision while keeping the metric hidden
from the agent. If two consecutive steps both trigger
($`\hat{d}_{k-1}<\tau`$ and $`\hat{d}_{k}<\tau`$), SPARK escalates to a
*strong* intervention that additionally withholds the previous *Next
Strategy* section and instructs the agent to anchor on *Verified Facts*
and *Current Error Pattern* rather than continuing the stale plan. The
full procedure, including the PDI-guided branch, is given in
<a href="#A8.SS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="H.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ Appendix H Pipeline Pseudocode ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1</span></span></a>; trajectory-level
case studies are also provided in <a href="#A3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix C Case Studies of Online PDI-Guided Control ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Downstream evaluation.

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate the skills generated <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">with and without PDI</span> control on
the same subset of tasks. This ablation directly tests whether the
trajectory-level signal can improve skill generation rather than merely
a post-hoc descriptor.
In <a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Effective skills ground in evidence rather than plans. ‣ 4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>, PDI-guided skills yield
stronger pass rates than their non-PDI counterparts. The largest
improvement appears on DeepSeek-Chat (pass rate from 9.1% to 42.4%).
These results indicate that the online intervention consistently
improves the downstream utility of distilled skills without introducing
negative side effects (case study in <a href="#A4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix D External Transfer Case Study: lean4-proof ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></span></a>). We further compare
SPARK against three skill generation baselines
(Trace2Skill \[<a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Trace2Skill: distill trajectory-local lessons into transferable agent skills">12</a>\],
AutoRefine \[<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref"
title="AutoRefine: from trajectories to reusable expertise for continual LLM agent refinement">15</a>\],
and EvoSkill \[<a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref"
title="EvoSkill: automated skill discovery for multi-agent systems">1</a>\])
under identical evaluation conditions; SPARK’s skill gain exceeds the
strongest baseline by $`+`$<!-- -->0.119 in mean reward
(<a href="#A10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix J Comparison with Baseline Skill Generation Methods ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></span></a>).

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Ablation Study on Task Variants

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

The main benchmark evaluates one skill on one task instance, leaving
robustness to various within-class instances untested. To assess this,
we generate 300 task variants via SPARK’s pipeline, preserving the
overall workflow while purposely resampling task-specific contents. This
design tests whether distilled skills encode reusable procedural
structure rather than overfitting to instance-specific surface form. In
<a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Effective skills ground in evidence rather than plans. ‣ 4.2.5 Posterior Distillation Index (PDI) ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>, SPARK retains positive
gains that the generated skill improves over the baseline by 3.3–5%
across all stdent models, confirming that distilled skills generalize
across instances within the same problem class. For cross-domain
generalization, we extend to evaluate SPARK on
ALFWorld \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref"
title="ALFWorld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">18</a>\],
a text-based interactive household environment that differs
fundamentally from programming tasks. PDI-refined skills improve overall
success rate from 16.7% to 40.0%, validating both the SPARK pipeline and
PDI in an out-of-distribution setting (<a href="#A11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix K External Benchmark: ALFWorld ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></span></a>).

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">

Skill generation and validation through the lens of trajectory quality
are crucial to advance agentic system. In this study, our central
contribution is the Posterior Distillation Index (PDI): an
interpretable, process-grounded criterion that enables a
trajectory-level measure of whether a generated skill is grounded in the
task environment rather than relying on prior plans. We demonstrate that
the SPARK framework can produce such trajectories and a PDI proxy can
guide and improve skill generation online. Together, autonomous skill
generation works strongly when agent learns from the environment as a
prerequisite, not an afterthought, for producing vital knowledge that
future agents can inherit and execute verifiably and reliably.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A1" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Positioning Against Prior Skill-Centric Systems

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#A1.T3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix A Positioning Against Prior Skill-Centric Systems ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> positions SPARK relative to
recent skill-centric systems along five dimensions. Prior work has
typically focused on only a subset of these properties: some methods
emphasize environment-grounded interaction, others study usefulness
evaluation or cross-model transfer, but few go beyond demonstrating that
skills can be produced or applied. In contrast, SPARK is designed not
only to generate transferable skills in executable environments, but
also to analyze why some trajectories yield useful downstream skills
while others do not. This trajectory-level mechanistic perspective
further enables analysis-guided online intervention, making SPARK
distinct from prior systems that treat skill generation primarily as a
black-box pipeline.

</div>
