<div id="A2" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Trajectory Feature Correlation Analysis

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Figure <a href="#A2.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 6 ‣ How to read the figure. ‣ Appendix B Trajectory Feature Correlation Analysis ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents a Spearman
rank-correlation heatmap between 23 trajectory-level features and the
downstream skill gain $`\Delta r_{m,t}`$ observed for each student
model. Each cell reports the Spearman $`\rho`$ between a feature
(column) and $`\Delta r_{m,t}`$ (row) computed over all tasks where
(i) the baseline student failed ($`r^{\text{base}}_{m,t}=0`$) and (ii) a
SPARK skill was available. The bottom row (<span id="A2.p1.10.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pooled</span>) aggregates all (task,
student) pairs across all seven student models. Significance levels are
annotated as $`\ast`$ ($`p<.05`$), $`\ast\ast`$ ($`p<.01`$), and
$`\ast\ast\ast`$ ($`p<.001`$). Red cells indicate that higher feature
values are associated with larger student gains; blue cells indicate the
opposite.

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### How to read the figure.

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Columns are grouped into four categories by colour: *Exploration
Dynamics* (blue), *Memo Quality* (green), *Skill Structure* (purple),
and *Non-predictive* (grey). A feature that shows consistent red across
most student rows and a significant pooled $`\rho`$ is a robust positive
predictor of skill usefulness; consistent blue indicates a negative
predictor. Features in the *Non-predictive* block were hypothesized to
matter but showed weak or inconsistent correlations, serving as negative
controls.

</div>

<figure id="A2.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x8.png" id="A2.F6.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="660"
height="275" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6:
</span>Spearman rank correlation between trajectory-level features
(columns) and student skill gain <span
class="math inline"><em>Δ</em><em>r</em><sub><em>m</em>, <em>t</em></sub></span>
(rows). Each row corresponds to a student model; the bottom row pools
all (task, model) pairs. Significance: <span
class="math inline">*</span> <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> &lt; .05</span>, <span
class="math inline">**</span> <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> &lt; .01</span>, <span
class="math inline">* * *</span> <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> &lt; .001</span>.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Feature definitions.

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Let $`\tau=(\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K})`$ denote the sequence of $`K`$
execution attempts for a task, $`\mu_{k}`$ the exploration memo after
the $`k`$-th reflect step, and $`s`$ the generated skill text. We use
$`\mathrm{tok}(\cdot)`$ for word-level tokenization and
$`\mathrm{J}(a,b)=|W_{a}\cap W_{b}|/|W_{a}\cup W_{b}|`$ for the Jaccard
similarity between word sets $`W_{a}`$ and $`W_{b}`$.

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx1" class="section ltx_subparagraph">

###### Exploration Dynamics.

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="A2.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compression
  ratio</span>: $`\rho_{c}=\sum_{k}|\tau_{k}^{\text{stdout}}|\;/\;|s|`$.
  Total raw agent output divided by skill length, matching the main-text
  definition in
  <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
  title="4.2.2 Does More Evidence or More Attempts Improve Skills? ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
  class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.2</span></a>.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reward
  variance</span>: $`\mathrm{Var}(\{r_{1},\dots,r_{K}\})`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First-retry
  reward gain</span>: $`\Delta r^{(1)}=r_{2}-r_{1}`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i4.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strategy
  pivot count</span>:
  $`\sum_{k=2}^{K}\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{J}(\text{strategy}_{k-1},\text{strategy}_{k})<0.15]`$,
  where $`\text{strategy}_{k}`$ is the “Next Strategy” section of
  $`\mu_{k}`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error-type
  shift count</span>: same as above, applied to the “Current Error
  Pattern” section.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx2" class="section ltx_subparagraph">

###### Memo Quality.

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="A2.I2.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memo lexical
  entropy</span>: $`\bar{H}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}H(\mu_{k})`$, where
  $`H(\mu_{k})=-\sum_{w}p_{w}\log_{2}p_{w}`$ is the Shannon entropy over
  word frequencies.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memo length
  growth rate</span>: $`(|\mu_{K}|-|\mu_{1}|)/|\mu_{1}|`$. Fractional
  increase in memo character count.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Negation-fact count</span>: number of
  bullet items in the final “Verified Facts” section matching negation
  keywords (<span id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1.2"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">not</span>,
  <span id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1.3"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">never</span>,
  <span id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1.4"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">failed</span>,
  <span id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1.5"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wrong</span>, etc.).

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Final
  verified-fact count</span>: total bullet items in the final “Verified
  Facts” section.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Per-step
  fact accrual</span>:
  $`\frac{1}{K{-}1}\sum_{k=2}^{K}(n_{k}^{\text{facts}}-n_{k-1}^{\text{facts}})`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i6"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error
  diagnosis specificity</span>: mean ratio of concrete references
  (inline code, numbers, file paths) to total words in the “Current
  Error Pattern” section across all memos.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx3" class="section ltx_subparagraph">

###### Skill Structure.

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="A2.I3.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill
  section count</span>: number of Markdown heading lines
  (<span id="A2.I3.i1.p1.1.2"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\#</span>,
  <span id="A2.I3.i1.p1.1.3"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\##</span>, …) in $`s`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I3.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill
  numbered-step count</span>: number of lines matching the pattern
  <span id="A2.I3.i2.p1.1.2"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/^\d+\[.)\]/</span> in $`s`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I3.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i3.p1.2.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill-to-command length ratio</span>:
  $`|s|\;/\;\overline{|\mathbf{c}_{\text{succ}}|}`$, where
  $`\overline{|\mathbf{c}_{\text{succ}}|}`$ is the mean character length
  of successful-attempt agent commands.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx4" class="section ltx_subparagraph">

###### Non-predictive (negative controls).

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="A2.I4.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill
  lexical density</span>:
  $`|\mathrm{unique}(\mathrm{tok}(s))|/|\mathrm{tok}(s)|`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill
  code-block ratio</span>: total characters inside
  <span id="A2.I4.i2.p1.1.2"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘‘…‘‘‘</span> blocks divided by
  $`|s|`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Final-memo
  pair similarity</span>: $`\mathrm{J}(\mu_{K-1},\mu_{K})`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Per-step
  3-gram novelty</span>: mean fraction of new word 3-grams at each memo
  step.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cumulative
  info gain</span>: sum of per-step 3-gram novelty across all steps.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i6"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test-stuck
  ratio</span>: fraction of consecutive attempt pairs with identical
  test summaries.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i7"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memo
  action-item count</span>: mean number of bullet/numbered items per
  memo.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i8"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i8.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i8.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill$`\leftrightarrow`$memo
  overlap</span>: $`\mathrm{J}(s,\mu_{K})`$.

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I4.i9"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I4.i9.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I4.i9.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill$`\leftrightarrow`$cmd
  overlap</span>: $`\mathrm{J}(s,\mathbf{c}_{\text{succ}})`$.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Case Studies of Online PDI-Guided Control

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We provide two trajectory-level case studies that compare PDI-enabled
runs against observe-only controls on <span id="A3.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">3d-scan-calc</span> and
<span id="A3.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">manufacturing-codebook-normalization</span>.
In <span id="A3.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">3d-scan-calc</span>, the weighted
proxy-PDI triggers a soft intervention at step 4 and escalates to a
strong one at step 5; the trajectory then rebounds to a clearly positive
regime, whereas the observe-only control keeps drifting downward. In
<span id="A3.p1.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">manufacturing-codebook-normalization</span>,
two earlier soft triggers (steps 3 and 5) already suffice to reverse the
decline and sustain positive proxy-PDI, while the control again stays
persistently negative. Together, these cases show that proxy-PDI is not
merely descriptive but an actionable online signal: it detects
plan-repetitive or stale-summary exploration and supports graded,
prompt-only interventions that redirect search without exposing the
metric to the model.

</div>

<figure id="A3.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2605.09192/assets/x9.png" id="A3.F7.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="660"

case studies of online PDI-guided control, comparing PDI-enabled runs

class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">3d-scan-calc</span> and <span
id="A3.F7.10.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">manufacturing-codebook-normalization</span>.
Each panel plots execution grounding (<span
class="math inline"><em>ϕ</em><sub>exec</sub></span>), plan copying
(<span class="math inline"><em>ϕ</em><sub>plan</sub></span>), memo
ossification (<span
class="math inline"><em>ϕ</em><sub>oss</sub></span>), and the
warmup-weighted proxy-PDI used for intervention decisions. Vertical
dashed lines mark soft and strong triggers.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div id="A4" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>External Transfer Case Study: <span id="A4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lean4-proof</span>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">

Among all tasks evaluated under PDI-refined skills, <span id="A4.p1.2.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lean4-proof</span> exhibits the
clearest behavioural shift in a held-out student model (Claude
Haiku 4.5, never used during skill generation or PDI refinement). The
task requires proving $`S\,n\leq 2`$ for the geometric-series sequence
$`S\,0=1,\;S\,(n{+}1)=S\,n+1/2^{n+1}`$ in Lean 4; the proof body must
start at line 15 of <span id="A4.p1.2.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">solution.lean</span>, and the
verifier runs <span id="A4.p1.2.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lake env lean -DwarningAsError=true
solution.lean</span> with zero output indicating success. We present the
analysis in three tables that progressively zoom in: skill-level
differences (<a href="#A4.T4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix D External Transfer Case Study: lean4-proof ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 4</span></a>), step-by-step
trajectory comparison
(<a href="#A4.T5" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix D External Transfer Case Study: lean4-proof ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>), and the resulting
strategy and score changes
(<a href="#A4.T6" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix D External Transfer Case Study: lean4-proof ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 6</span></a>).

</div>

shift and quantitative changes induced by the PDI-refined skill on <span
id="A4.T6.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lean4-proof</span>.

cues that drive each behavioural change. The bottom rows report

PDI-refined skills compensate for capability gaps by converting
posterior evidence into executable recipes.</figcaption>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Why PDI made the difference.

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

The non-PDI skill tells the agent *what* to prove (closed-form identity
$`\to`$ bound) but not *how* to write the Lean 4 tactics. The
PDI-refined skill was generated after observing that weaker models fail
precisely at the tactic level, so it includes: (1) the exact
<span id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">simp \[S\]</span> +
<span id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ring</span> pattern for the
inductive step; (2) the <span id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">norm_num</span> +
<span id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">linarith</span> pattern for the
bound derivation; and (3) a “test in <span id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/tmp</span> first” workflow that
prevents corrupting the solution file. This is the PDI mechanism in
action: by comparing successful and failed trajectories across models,
the refinement process identifies *where agents actually get stuck* and
injects targeted procedural knowledge. The result is not merely a longer
document, but a fundamentally different *action policy* for the student:
the original skill transfers a plan; the PDI-refined skill transfers an
execution recipe anchored in verified evidence.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A5" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Sensitivity of PDI to the Smoothing Parameter

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">

The smoothing constant $`\alpha`$ in
<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="4.2.4 What Separates Useful Iterative Skills from Useless Ones? ‣ 4.2 Trajectory-Level Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4.2.4</span></a> controls the
sharpness of the empirical token distributions: smaller $`\alpha`$
yields distributions closer to raw frequency counts, while larger
$`\alpha`$ flattens them toward uniform.
<a href="#A5.F8" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix E Sensitivity of PDI to the Smoothing Parameter ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 8</span></a> reports the Spearman
$`\rho`$ and $`p`$-values of PDI across $`\alpha\in[10^{-10},10]`$. All
three correlation metrics (task-level, pair-level, and pass-gain)
exhibit a plateau for $`\alpha\lesssim 10^{-3}`$, where smoothing is
negligible relative to observed counts, and degrade monotonically as
$`\alpha`$ increases beyond $`10^{-2}`$. The Mann–Whitney U test between
high- and low-PDI groups remains significant ($`p{<}0.05`$) for
$`\alpha\leq 0.005`$ and loses significance for $`\alpha\geq 0.007`$.
This pattern confirms that PDI is robust to the choice of $`\alpha`$
within a broad low-smoothing regime.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A6" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Sensitivity of PDI to Component Weights

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">

PDI combines three z-scored components with equal weights:
$`\mathrm{PDI}=z(\phi_{\mathrm{exec}})-z(\phi_{\mathrm{plan}})-z(\phi_{\mathrm{oss}})`$.
We examine whether this choice is justified by testing (i) whether the
directional structure itself is robust, (ii) whether fitted weights
generalize across held-out models and tasks, and (iii) whether each
component is necessary.

</div>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Directional structure.

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We sweep all weight combinations $`(w_{e},w_{p},w_{o})`$ with
$`w_{e}>0`$ (preserving the sign convention that execution grounding
contributes positively while plan copying and memo ossification
contribute negatively). The large majority of sign-consistent
combinations yield statistically significant Spearman correlation
($`p{<}0.05`$) with student skill gain, indicating that PDI’s predictive
power derives from its directional structure rather than from any
particular weight assignment.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Cross-validated weight stability.

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

To test whether fitted weights generalize, we perform 5-fold task
cross-validation: on each fold, we grid-search the weight vector that
maximizes Spearman $`\rho`$ on the training tasks and evaluate it on the
held-out fold. <a href="#A6.T7" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 7 ‣ Cross-validated weight stability. ‣ Appendix F Sensitivity of PDI to Component Weights ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a> reports the results.
Grid search produces four distinct “optimal” weight vectors across five
folds, yet equal weighting matches or exceeds the fitted optimum on
every fold (5/5). A complementary leave-one-model-out protocol yields a
similar pattern: nine folds produce five distinct optimal vectors.
Together, these results confirm that weight tuning does not yield
transferable gains and that the fitted optimum is an artifact of the
particular train split.

</div>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Component ablation.

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Removing execution grounding ($`w_{e}{=}0`$) collapses held-out
correlation to near zero; removing memo ossification ($`w_{o}{=}0`$)
also degrades predictive power. Equal weighting thus serves as a
principled, parameter-free default that preserves all three empirically
validated directional signals without introducing tunable
hyperparameters that risk overfitting to a particular task or model
distribution.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A7" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Exploration Statistics

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#A7.T8" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix G Exploration Statistics ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> summarises the exploration
cost of the SPARK skill-generation pipeline across four teacher models.
All models share the same task pool and Docker-based execution
environment; the maximum retry budget $`N_{\max}`$ is 7 for Claude Opus
4.6, GPT-5.2-Codex, GPT-5.4 and GLM-5. These figures should be
interpreted as an upfront investment in capability transfer rather than
a per-query serving cost: strong interactive teachers are expensive to
run repeatedly, but once their trajectories are distilled into reusable
<span id="A7.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span> documents, the same
procedural knowledge can be deployed to much cheaper student models at
inference time. In this sense, SPARK trades one-time high-cost
exploration for repeated low-cost execution. The main-text results show
that this trade can be favorable not only economically but also in
effectiveness, since several skill-equipped students even surpass the
interaction-free performance of the stronger teacher models.

</div>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Student inference cost and amortization.

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

While teacher exploration is expensive, the distilled skills are
consumed by much cheaper student models at inference time.
<a href="#A7.T9" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 9 ‣ Student inference cost and amortization. ‣ Appendix G Exploration Statistics ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 9</span></a> reports the per-task
inference cost of representative student models, computed from the
token-level usage logs recorded in each evaluation trajectory. Across
all measured students, the per-task cost ranges from \$0.02
(DeepSeek-Chat) to \$0.18 (GLM-4.5-Air), yielding 86-task totals between
\$1.89 and \$15.48. Compared with the cheapest teacher (GLM-5 at
\$9.90/task), even the most expensive student is $`55\times`$ cheaper
per task; DeepSeek-Chat is over $`1{,}100\times`$ cheaper than Claude
Opus 4.6. A single teacher exploration run (\$852–\$2,126 for 86 tasks)
can therefore be amortized over hundreds of student deployments at
negligible marginal cost.

</div>

<div id="A8" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Pipeline Pseudocode

<div id="A8.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Skill Generation Pipeline

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Algorithm <a href="#alg1" class="ltx_ref"
title="Algorithm 1 ‣ H.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ Appendix H Pipeline Pseudocode ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> describes the iterative
skill-generation loop introduced in
<a href="#S3.SS1" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.1 Skill Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.1</span></a>. The teacher model
explores each task inside a containerized sandbox for up to $`N_{\max}`$
attempts. Failed attempts trigger a <span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reflect</span> step that rewrites
the exploration memo; a successful attempt triggers evidence assembly
and skill distillation.

</div>

class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

</div>

<div id="A8.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.2 </span>Task Construction Pipeline

<div id="A8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Algorithm <a href="#alg2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Algorithm 2 ‣ H.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ Appendix H Pipeline Pseudocode ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> details the task-construction
pipeline (<a href="#S3.SS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.2</span></a>). A natural-language
prompt is expanded into a structured blueprint, iteratively critiqued
and repaired, rendered into a runnable task directory, and validated by
executing the oracle inside the target Docker environment.

</div>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1" class="section ltx_subsubsection">

#### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">H.2.1 </span>Integrated Techniques for Exploration Quality

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

SPARK integrates several complementary techniques that improve
exploration efficiency and distillation fidelity. To reduce noise in the
skill-generation context, it applies a lightweight command-processing
pipeline: each command is (i) classified into one of five semantic
categories (<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Verify</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Implement</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Inspect</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Prepare</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Action</span>), (ii) scored by a
keyword-weighted importance function that prioritizes verification and
implementation actions, and (iii) filtered to remove low-signal commands
(e.g., <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ls</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.7"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pwd</span>,
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.8"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">echo</span>). Multi-line commands
that match known domain patterns (e.g., spreadsheet manipulation via
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.3.9"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">openpyxl</span>, PDDL planning,
bibliographic API queries) are replaced with semantic summaries. The
top-$`k`$ commands (default $`k{=}12`$) are selected by score and
presented in execution order, yielding a concise yet high-signal
execution chain. In addition, as the agent approaches $`N_{\max}`$,
retry injection adds an escalating urgency signal.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>Generated Task Examples

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">

We present three tasks produced by the SPARK task-construction pipeline
(<a href="#S3.SS2" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="3.2 Task Construction Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3.2</span></a>) to illustrate the
diversity and self-contained nature of the generated benchmarks. Each
task was created from a short natural-language prompt, automatically
expanded into a full blueprint, critiqued, repaired, and validated by
executing the oracle inside the target Docker environment. No manual
editing was performed after generation.

</div>

<div id="A9.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.1 </span>3D Scan Mass Calculation

<div id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Prompt (input).

<div id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

*“Calculate the mass of a 3D printed part from a binary STL scan. The
2-byte Attribute Byte Count field stores the Material ID. Filter out
scanning debris by keeping only the largest connected component, look up
the density, and output the mass.”*

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Generated task.

<div id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

The pipeline produces a complete task directory containing: (i) an
<span id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">instruction.md</span> that asks the
agent to parse a binary STL file, identify the largest connected
component of the triangle mesh, extract the Material ID from the
attribute field, look up the corresponding density from a provided
material table, compute the volume via the signed-tetrahedron method,
and write the result to a JSON file; (ii) a
<span id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">build_data.py</span> script that
deterministically synthesizes the STL asset and material table during
Docker build; (iii) a pytest oracle that checks the reported mass within
0.1% relative tolerance.

</div>

<div id="A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">

This task exercises binary file parsing, computational geometry
(connected components, mesh volume), and multi-source data integration,
a combination unlikely to be solved by template matching alone.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.2 </span>WAV Amplitude Analysis

<div id="A9.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Prompt (input).

<div id="A9.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

*“Parse a binary WAV file, split it into 1-second segments, compute the
RMS amplitude of each segment, and identify the loudest one.”*

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Generated task.

<div id="A9.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

The agent must read a WAV file using only Python’s standard library,
segment the audio by sample rate, compute per-segment RMS values, and
produce a structured JSON report including sample rate, channel count,
duration, per-segment statistics, and the index of the loudest segment.
The oracle verifies all numeric fields within 0.01% relative tolerance.
The audio asset is synthesized deterministically during environment
build, ensuring reproducibility without distributing binary data.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.3 </span>Weather Station Anomaly Detection

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Prompt (input).

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

*“Detect anomalous hourly temperature readings across multiple weather
stations using a 3$`\sigma`$ threshold.”*

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Generated task.

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

The pipeline generates a CSV dataset containing hourly readings from
multiple stations with injected anomalies. The agent must compute
per-station population statistics, flag readings beyond three standard
deviations, and output a JSON report with station count, total readings,
anomaly count, and a timestamp-sorted anomaly list. The oracle validates
both aggregate counts and per-anomaly fields. This task requires careful
attention to specification details (population vs. sample standard
deviation, strict vs. non-strict inequality, and per-station
independence) that are common sources of silent errors.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Observations.

<div id="A9.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Across all three examples, the pipeline consistently produces tasks that
are (i) fully self-contained (all assets are built deterministically at
Docker build time), (ii) oracle-validated (the solution script passes
the pytest verifier before the task is accepted), and (iii) non-trivial
(each requires domain-specific reasoning beyond simple text
manipulation). These properties make the generated tasks suitable for
both skill-generation training and downstream evaluation.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A10" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>Comparison with Baseline Skill Generation Methods

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">

To further validate the effectiveness of PDI-guided SPARK, we compare
against three recent skill generation methods,
Trace2Skill \[<a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Trace2Skill: distill trajectory-local lessons into transferable agent skills">12</a>\],
AutoRefine \[<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref"
title="AutoRefine: from trajectories to reusable expertise for continual LLM agent refinement">15</a>\],
and EvoSkill \[<a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref"
title="EvoSkill: automated skill discovery for multi-agent systems">1</a>\],
on the SkillsBench task suite. All methods use the same skill generation
model (<span id="A10.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude-sonnet-4</span>) and the
same evaluation pipeline (student model: <span id="A10.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">deepseek-chat</span>; agent
framework: <span id="A10.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">qwen-coder</span>; timeout
multiplier: 0.5; Docker-based Harbor sandbox). The skill gain $`\Delta`$
is the primary comparison metric, as it controls for baseline
stochasticity across independent runs.

</div>

<div id="A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Reproduction details.

<div id="A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We re-implement each baseline following its published algorithm. Key
configuration parameters are summarized in
<a href="#A10.T10" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 10 ‣ Reproduction details. ‣ Appendix J Comparison with Baseline Skill Generation Methods ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 10</span></a>.

</div>

<div id="A10.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Results.

<div id="A10.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#A10.T11" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 11 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix J Comparison with Baseline Skill Generation Methods ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 11</span></a> reports the comparison.
SPARK achieves the highest $`\Delta`$ Pass Rate ($`+`$<!-- -->28.8%) and
$`\Delta`$ MR ($`+`$<!-- -->0.291), outperforming the strongest baseline
AutoRefine by $`+`$<!-- -->10.2% in pass rate gain and
$`+`$<!-- -->0.119 in mean reward gain. SPARK also exhibits the most
favorable improvement-to-degradation ratio (21 improved vs. 3 degraded
tasks), whereas AutoRefine improves 19 tasks but degrades 9. These
results confirm that PDI-guided posterior distillation produces
substantially stronger skills than methods that rely on lesson
extraction, iterative refinement, or evolutionary search without
environment-grounded trajectory analysis.

</div>

<div id="A11" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix K </span>External Benchmark: ALFWorld

<div id="A11.p1" class="ltx_para">

To evaluate whether SPARK generalizes beyond terminal-based programming
tasks, we conduct an external evaluation on
ALFWorld \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref"
title="ALFWorld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">18</a>\],
a text-based interactive household environment where agents issue
natural-language commands to manipulate objects. ALFWorld differs
fundamentally from SkillsBench: actions are discrete text commands
rather than shell operations, feedback is environment state descriptions
rather than program output, and success requires multi-step physical
reasoning. This evaluation simultaneously validates both the SPARK skill
generation pipeline and the PDI-guided refinement mechanism in an
out-of-distribution setting.

</div>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Setup.

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate on the ALFWorld <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">eval_out_of_distribution</span>
split (134 games, 6 task types). The agent framework is ReAct (1-shot,
per task type) with a maximum of 30 steps per game.
<a href="#A11.T12" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 12 ‣ Setup. ‣ Appendix K External Benchmark: ALFWorld ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 12</span></a> summarizes the
evaluation configuration.

</div>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Skill generation and PDI refinement.

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

For each teacher, we run 30 exploration games and collect trajectories.
Skills are distilled per task type under two conditions: without PDI
filtering and with PDI-guided trajectory selection. PDI scores are
computed per trajectory; the PDI condition prioritizes high-PDI
trajectories during distillation.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Results.

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#A11.T13" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 13 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix K External Benchmark: ALFWorld ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 13</span></a> and
<a href="#A11.T14" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"
title="Table 14 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix K External Benchmark: ALFWorld ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 14</span></a> report per-task-type
success rates for the two teacher models. Under both teachers,
SPARK-generated skills improve overall success rate over the no-skill
baseline, and PDI-guided skills consistently outperform their non-PDI
counterparts. With GPT-5.5 as teacher, PDI-refined skills achieve 40.0%
overall success (vs. 16.7% baseline), with gains appearing even on task
types where the teacher itself never succeeded during exploration (e.g.,
Pick & Place, Cool & Place), indicating that PDI-guided distillation can
extract transferable procedural patterns from partial successes in
related task types. For brevity, we omit *Heat & Place* and *Pick Two*
from the tables, since the baseline is already 0% and all three
conditions remain at 0% (no change, neither gain nor drop).

</div>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Reproduction.

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

All experiments use the ALFWorld Python package
(<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pip install alfworld</span>) with
the default <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">eval_out_of_distribution</span>
split. Teacher exploration runs with 10 parallel workers. Skill
distillation uses <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude-sonnet-4.5</span> with and
without the PDI flag. Student evaluation runs across 3 conditions with
10 parallel workers per condition. Scripts are located in
<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">extra/benchmark/scripts/</span>:
<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">launch_parallel.py</span> (teacher
exploration), <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">skill_gen.py</span> (distillation),
<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.7"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">launch_parallel_eval.py</span>
(student evaluation), and <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.8"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">generate_tables.py</span> (result
aggregation).

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A12" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix L </span>Limitations and Scope

<div id="A12.p1" class="ltx_para">

Our study focuses on text- and terminal-based agent environments and
validates SPARK on SkillsBench, 300 SPARK-generated task variants, and
the out-of-distribution ALFWorld benchmark. Extending the same
trajectory-level analysis to other agent modalities (e.g., GUI-based or
multi-modal settings) is a natural direction that we leave for future
work. PDI is intentionally instantiated as a simple, equal-weight linear
composite of three interpretable signals, which we find to be a robust
default across held-out folds (<a href="#A6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix F Sensitivity of PDI to Component Weights ‣ Evidence Over Plans: Online Trajectory Verification for Skill Distillation">Appendix <span
class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></span></a>); a fully learned or
domain-adapted variant may be beneficial when a large, homogeneous task
distribution is available.

</div>
